The figure below shows an example of ReAct and the different steps involved to perform question answering.</p><div class="mt-7"><img loading="eager" alt="None" class="pt-5 m-auto lightense-target" role="presentation" referrerpolicy="no-referrer" src="https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/0*ZHi3mQltFI51mEV-"></div><figcaption class="mt-3 text-sm text-center text-gray-500 dark:text-gray-200"><a style="text-decoration: underline;" rel="noopener" title="" href="https://www.promptingguide.ai/techniques/react" target="_blank">Source</a></figcaption><h3 id="0219" class="font-bold font-sans break-normal text-gray-900 dark:text-gray-100 text-1xl md:text-2xl pt-12">Model Optimization Techniques</h3><div class="mt-7"><img loading="eager" alt="None" class="pt-5 m-auto lightense-target" role="presentation" referrerpolicy="no-referrer" src="https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/0*TUFXJ5K8mKeXT_qo"></div><figcaption class="mt-3 text-sm text-center text-gray-500 dark:text-gray-200"><a style="text-decoration: underline;" rel="" title="" href="https://www.qualcomm.com/news/onq/2023/12/optimizing-generative-ai-for-edge-devices" target="_blank">Source</a></figcaption><div class="mt-7"><img loading="eager" alt="None" class="pt-5 m-auto lightense-target" role="presentation" referrerpolicy="no-referrer" src="https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*E6836BTl2oZj-cw21mURKA.jpeg"></div><figcaption class="mt-3 text-sm text-center text-gray-500 dark:text-gray-200"><a style="text-decoration: underline;" rel="" title="" href="https://www.researchgate.net/figure/Model-compression-methods-a-pruning-b-quantization-and-c-knowledge-distillation_fig2_372897065" target="_blank">Model compression methods: (a) pruning, (b) quantization, and © knowledge distillation</a></figcaption><h4 id="caa5" class="font-bold font-sans break-normal text-gray-900 dark:text-gray-100 text-l md:text-xl pt-8">Quantization</h4><p class="leading-8 mt-3"><strong>Model Quantization is a technique used to reduce the size of large neural networks, including large language models (LLMs) by modifying the precision of their weights. </strong>LLM<strong> </strong>Quantization is enabled thanks to empiric results showing that while some operations related to neural network training and inference must leverage high precision, in some cases it's possible to use significantly lower precision (float16 for example) reducing the overall size of the model, allowing it to be run using less powerful hardware with an <strong>acceptable reduction of its capabilities and accuracy</strong>.</p><div class="mt-7"><img loading="eager" alt="None" class="pt-5 m-auto lightense-target" role="presentation" referrerpolicy="no-referrer" src="https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/0*gsfyBupkCQF1Igfs.png"></div><figcaption class="mt-3 text-sm text-center text-gray-500 dark:text-gray-200">Trend of model sizes | AWS reinvent</figcaption><p class="leading-8 mt-7"><strong>Precision Trade-off</strong></p><div class="mt-7"><img loading="eager" alt="None" class="pt-5 m-auto lightense-target" role="presentation" referrerpolicy="no-referrer" src="https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/0*26dUUfrnCjawSq2g.png"></div><figcaption class="mt-3 text-sm text-center text-gray-500 dark:text-gray-200">Tensors | <a style="text-decoration: underline;" rel="" title="" href="https://www.tensorops.ai/post/what-are-quantized-llms" target="_blank">Source</a></figcaption><p class="leading-8 mt-7">Generally, using high precision in neural networks is associated with better accuracy and more stable training(read more about it <a style="text-decoration: underline;" rel="noopener noreferrer" title="" href="https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/performance/mixed-precision-training/index.html" target="_blank">here</a>). Using high precision is also more computationally expensive as it requires <strong>more hardware</strong> and more <strong>expensive hardware</strong>. Research mostly done by Google and NVIDIA regarding the possibility of using lower precision for some neural network operations showed that lower precision can be leveraged for some training and inference operations.</p><p class="leading-8 mt-7">Aside from the research, both companies developed hardware and frameworks to support lower precision operations. For example, the NVIDIA T4 accelerators are lower precision GPUs with Tensor Cores technology that is significantly more efficient than that of the K80. Google's TPUs introduced the concept of bfloat16, a special primitive data type optimized for neural networks. <strong>The fundamental idea behind lower precision is that neural networks don't always need to use ALL the range that 64-bit floats to allow them to perform well.</strong></p><div class="mt-7"><img loading="eager" alt="None" class="pt-5 m-auto lightense-target" role="presentation" referrerpolicy="no-referrer" src="https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/0*YfyNqBcu-b_AG6Vk.png"></div><figcaption class="mt-3 text-sm text-center text-gray-500 dark:text-gray-200">The bfloat16 numerical format | Google</figcaption><p class="leading-8 mt-7">As neural networks became increasingly large, the importance of leveraging lower precision had a significant impact on the ability to use them. With LLMs, this became even more crucial.</p><p class="leading-8 mt-7">For reference, an A100 GPU by Nvidia has 80GB of memory in its most advanced version. In the table below we can see that the LLama2–70B model requires 138 GB of memory approximately, meaning that to host it, we will need multiple A100s. Distributing models over multiple GPUs means paying for more GPUs as well as overhead infrastructure. A quantized version, on the other hand, requires around 40 GB of memory, therefore it can fit easily into one A100, reducing the cost of inference significantly. This example doesn't even mention the fact that within the single A100, using quantized models would result in faster execution of most of the individual computation operations.</p><div class="mt-7"><img loading="eager" alt="None" class="pt-5 m-auto lightense-target" role="presentation" referrerpolicy="no-referrer" src="https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*OzXqLwEn4lH9yMGVued5gA.png"></div><figcaption class="mt-3 text-sm text-center text-gray-500 dark:text-gray-200"><a style="text-decoration: underline;" rel="noopener" title="" href="https://www.tensorops.ai/post/what-are-quantized-llms" target="_blank">Example of 4-bit quantization using llama.cpp, size may vary slightly depending on the method</a></figcaption><p class="leading-8 mt-7"><strong>How does quantization shrink models?</strong></p><p class="leading-8 mt-7">Quantization significantly decreases the model's size by <strong>reducing the number of bits required for each model weight</strong>. A typical scenario would be the reduction of the weights from FP16 (16-bit Floating-point) to INT4 (4-bit Integer). This allows for models to run on <strong>cheaper hardware</strong> and/or with <strong>higher speed</strong>. By reducing the precision of the weights, the<strong> overall quality of the LLM can also suffer some impact</strong>.</p><p class="leading-8 mt-7">Studies show that this impact varies depending on the techniques used and that larger models suffer less from change in precision. Larger models (over ~70B) can maintain their capacities even when converted to 4-bit, with some <strong>techniques such as the NF4 suggesting no impact on their performance</strong>. Therefore, <strong>4-bit appears to be the best compromise</strong> between performance and size/speed for these <strong>larger models</strong>, while 6 or 8-bit might be better for smaller models.</p><p class="leading-8 mt-7"><strong>Types of LLM Quantization</strong></p><p class="leading-8 mt-7">It's possible to divide the techniques of obtaining quantized models into two:</p><ol class="pl-8 mt-2 list-decimal"><li class="mt-3"><strong>Post-Training Quantization (PTQ)</strong>: converting the weights of an already trained model to a lower precision without any retraining. Though straightforward and easy to implement, PTQ might degrade the model's performance slightly due to the loss of precision in the value of the weights.</li><li class="mt-3"><strong>Quantization-Aware Training (QAT)</strong>: Unlike PTQ, QAT integrates the weight conversion process during the training stage. This often results in superior model performance, but it's more computationally demanding. A highly used QAT technique is the <a style="text-decoration: underline;" rel="noopener noreferrer" title="" href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14314" target="_blank">QLoRA</a>.</li></ol><div class="mt-7"><img loading="eager" alt="None" class="pt-5 m-auto lightense-target" role="presentation" referrerpolicy="no-referrer" src="https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/0*7CAakpTb4twXGVdW.jpg"></div><p class="leading-8 mt-7">This post will only focus on <strong>PTQ</strong> strategies and the key distinctions between them.</p><p class="leading-8 mt-7"><strong>Larger Quantized Model vs Smaller Non-Quantized</strong></p><p class="leading-8 mt-7">Acknowledging that reducing the precision will reduce the accuracy of the model, should you prefer a <strong>smaller full-precision model</strong> or a <strong>larger quantized model</strong> with a comparable inference cost? Although the ideal choice might vary due to diverse factors, recent <a style="text-decoration: underline;" rel="noopener noreferrer" title="" href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.17888" target="_blank">research</a> by Meta offers some insightful guidelines.</p><p class="leading-8 mt-7">While we expect that reducing the precision would result in the reduction of the accuracy, Meta researchers have demonstrated that in some cases, not only does the <strong>quantized model demonstrate superior performance</strong>, but it also allows for <strong>reduced latency</strong> and enhanced throughput. The same trend can be observed when comparing an <strong>8-bit 13B model with a 16-bit 7B model</strong>. In essence, when comparing models with similar inference costs, <strong>the larger quantized models can outperform their smaller, non-quantized counterparts</strong>. This advantage becomes even more pronounced with larger networks, as they exhibit a smaller quality loss when quantized.</p><p class="leading-8 mt-7"><strong>Where to find already Quantized models?</strong></p><p class="leading-8 mt-7">Fortunately, it is possible to <strong>find many versions of models</strong> already quantized using <strong>GPTQ</strong> (some compatible with ExLLama), <strong>NF4</strong> or <strong>GGML</strong> on the <a style="text-decoration: underline;" rel="noopener noreferrer" title="" href="https://huggingface.co/models" target="_blank">Hugging Face Hub</a>. A quick glance would reveal that a substantial chunk of these models has been quantified by <a style="text-decoration: underline;" rel="noopener noreferrer" title="" href="https://huggingface.co/TheBloke" target="_blank">TheBloke</a>, an influential and respected figure in the LLM community. This user has published several models with different types of quantization methods so one can choose to use the best fit for each particular use-case.</p><p class="leading-8 mt-7">To easily experiment with these models open up a <a style="text-decoration: underline;" rel="noopener noreferrer" title="" href="https://colab.google/" target="_blank">Google Colab</a> and make sure you change your <strong>runtime to a GPU</strong> (a free one is available for use). Start by installing the transformers library maintained by Hugging Face and all necessary libraries. Since we will be using a model <strong>quantized using Auto-GPTQ</strong> the respective libraries will also be required:</p><pre class="flex flex-col justify-center border mt-7 dark:border-gray-700"><button class="p-1 bg-gray-300 hljs-copy dark:bg-zinc-800">Copy</button><code class="p-2 bg-gray-100 dark:bg-gray-900 overflow-x-auto language-python hljs" data-highlighted="yes">!pip install transformers
!pip install accelerate

<span class="hljs-comment"># Due to using GPTQ</span>
!pip install optimum
!pip install auto-gptq</code></pre><p class="leading-8 mt-7">You might need to restart the runtime so that the installs are available. Then simply load the already quantized model, in this case we are loading a Llama-2–7B-Chat <strong>model previously quantized</strong> using Auto-GPTQ, as shown below:</p><pre class="flex flex-col justify-center border mt-7 dark:border-gray-700"><button class="p-1 bg-gray-300 hljs-copy dark:bg-zinc-800">Copy</button><code class="p-2 bg-gray-100 dark:bg-gray-900 overflow-x-auto language-java hljs" data-highlighted="yes">from transformers <span class="hljs-keyword">import</span> AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
<span class="hljs-keyword">import</span> <span class="hljs-type">torch</span>

<span class="hljs-variable">model_id</span> <span class="hljs-operator">=</span> <span class="hljs-string">"TheBloke/Llama-2-7b-Chat-GPTQ"</span>
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id, torch_dtype=torch.float16, device_map=<span class="hljs-string">"auto"</span>)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, torch_dtype=torch.float16, device_map=<span class="hljs-string">"auto"</span>)</code></pre><p class="leading-8 mt-7"><strong>Quantizing a LLM</strong></p><p class="leading-8 mt-7">As highlighted earlier, a plethora of quantized models already reside on the <strong>Hugging Face Hub</strong>, eliminating the necessity to compress a model personally in many scenarios. However, in same cases you may want to <strong>use models which are not yet quantized</strong> or you may want to compress the model yourself. This can be achieved by using a dataset tailored to your specific domain.</p><p class="leading-8 mt-7">To demonstrate how to easily quantize a model using <strong>AutoGPTQ</strong> along with the Transformers library, we employed a streamlined variant of the AutoGPTQ interface found in Optimum — Hugging Face's solution for refining training and inference:</p><pre class="flex flex-col justify-center border mt-7 dark:border-gray-700"><button class="p-1 bg-gray-300 hljs-copy dark:bg-zinc-800">Copy</button><code class="p-2 bg-gray-100 dark:bg-gray-900 overflow-x-auto language-python hljs" data-highlighted="yes"><span class="hljs-keyword">from</span> transformers <span class="hljs-keyword">import</span> AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, GPTQConfig

model_id = <span class="hljs-string">"facebook/opt-125m"</span>

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)

quantization_config = GPTQConfig(bits=<span class="hljs-number">4</span>, dataset = <span class="hljs-string">"c4"</span>, tokenizer=tokenizer)

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, device_map=<span class="hljs-string">"auto"</span>, quantization_config=quantization_config)</code></pre><p class="leading-8 mt-7"><strong>Model compression can be time-consuming</strong>. For instance, a 175B model demands at least <strong>4 GPU hours</strong>, especially with expansive datasets like "c4". Notably, the number of bits in the quantization process or the dataset can be easily modified by the parameters of GPTQConfig. Changing the dataset will impact how the quantization is done so, if possible, <strong>use a dataset that resembles data seen in inference</strong> to maximize performance.</p><p class="leading-8 mt-7"><strong>Quantization Techniques</strong></p><div class="mt-7"><img loading="eager" alt="None" class="pt-5 m-auto lightense-target" role="presentation" referrerpolicy="no-referrer" src="https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/0*D2fGOxx-eCOxLFNV.png"></div><figcaption class="mt-3 text-sm text-center text-gray-500 dark:text-gray-200"><a style="text-decoration: underline;" rel="" title="" href="https://www.tensorops.ai/post/what-are-quantized-llms" target="_blank">Techniques</a></figcaption><p class="leading-8 mt-7">Several state-of-the-art methods have emerged in the arena of model quantization. Let's delve into some prominent ones:</p><ol class="pl-8 mt-2 list-decimal"><li class="mt-3"><strong>GPTQ:</strong> With some implementation options <a style="text-decoration: underline;" rel="noopener noreferrer" title="" href="https://github.com/PanQiWei/AutoGPTQ" target="_blank">AutoGPTQ</a>, <a style="text-decoration: underline;" rel="noopener noreferrer" title="" href="https://github.com/turboderp/exllama" target="_blank">ExLlama</a> and <a style="text-decoration: underline;" rel="noopener noreferrer" title="" href="https://github.com/qwopqwop200/GPTQ-for-LLaMa" target="_blank">GPTQ-for-LLaMa</a>, this method focuses mainly on GPU execution.</li><li class="mt-3"><strong>NF4:</strong> Being implemented on the <a style="text-decoration: underline;" rel="noopener noreferrer" title="" href="https://github.com/TimDettmers/bitsandbytes" target="_blank">bitsandbytes</a> library it works closely with the Hugging Face <a style="text-decoration: underline;" rel="noopener noreferrer" title="" href="https://github.com/huggingface/transformers" target="_blank">transformers</a> library. It is primarily <strong>used by QLoRA</strong> methods and loads models in 4-bit precision for fine-tuning.</li><li class="mt-3"><strong>GGML:</strong> This C library works closely with the llama.cpp library. It features a unique binary format for LLMs, allowing for fast loading and ease of reading. Notably, its recent <strong>shift to the GGUF format</strong> ensures future extensibility and compatibility.</li></ol><p class="leading-8 mt-7">Many quantization libraries support several different quantization strategies (e.g. 4-bit, 5-bit, and 8-bit quantization), each of which offers different trade-offs between efficiency and performance.</p><h4 id="0ec9" class="font-bold font-sans break-normal text-gray-900 dark:text-gray-100 text-l md:text-xl pt-8">Distillation</h4><div class="mt-7"><img loading="eager" alt="None" class="pt-5 m-auto lightense-target" role="presentation" referrerpolicy="no-referrer" src="https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/0*2JpoPAc2RR2eLNx-.png"></div><figcaption class="mt-3 text-sm text-center text-gray-500 dark:text-gray-200"><a style="text-decoration: underline;" rel="" title="" href="https://lilianweng.github.io/posts/2023-01-10-inference-optimization/" target="_blank">Source</a></figcaption><p class="leading-8 mt-7"><strong>Knowledge Distillation</strong> (<strong>KD</strong>; <a style="text-decoration: underline;" rel="" title="" href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.02531" target="_blank">Hinton et al. 2015</a>, <a style="text-decoration: underline;" rel="" title="" href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.05525" target="_blank">Gou et al. 2020</a>) is a straightforward way to build a smaller, cheaper model (<em>"student model"</em>) to speed up inference by transferring skills from a pre-trained expensive model (<em>"teacher model"</em>) into the student. There is no much restriction on how the student architecture should be constructed, except for a matched output space with the teacher to construct a proper learning objective.</p><div class="mt-7"><img loading="eager" alt="None" class="pt-5 m-auto lightense-target" role="presentation" referrerpolicy="no-referrer" src="https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/0*Yzu1tmAqUIUq3KrU.png"></div><figcaption class="mt-3 text-sm text-center text-gray-500 dark:text-gray-200"><a style="text-decoration: underline;" rel="" title="" href="https://techtalkverse.com/post/artificial-intelligence/llm-basics/#optimization-techniques" target="_blank">Distillation</a></figcaption><p class="leading-8 mt-7">The teacher model is already fine-tuned on the training data. So, the probability distribution likely closely matches the ground truth data and won't have many variations in tokens.</p><p class="leading-8 mt-7">So, when temperature &gt; 1 then, probability distribution becomes broader.
T &gt; 1 =&gt; Teacher's output –&gt; soft labels and Student's output –&gt; soft predictions
T = 1 =&gt; Teacher's output –&gt; hard labels and Student's output –&gt; hard predictions</p><p class="leading-8 mt-7"><code class="p-1.5 bg-gray-300 dark:bg-gray-600">Distillation is not as effective for generative decoder models. Its effective for encoder only models, such as BERT, which have a lot of representation redundancy.</code></p><h4 id="27f5" class="font-bold font-sans break-normal text-gray-900 dark:text-gray-100 text-l md:text-xl pt-8">Pruning</h4><p class="leading-8 mt-3">Network pruning is to reduce the model size by trimming unimportant model weights or connections while the model capacity remains. It may or may not require re-training. Pruning can be <strong>unstructured</strong> or <strong>structured</strong>.</p><ul class="pl-8 mt-2 list-disc"><li class="mt-3"><em>Unstructured pruning</em> is allowed to drop any weight or connection, so it does not retain the original network architecture. Unstructured pruning often does not work well with modern hardware and doesn't lead to actual inference speedup.</li><li class="mt-3"><em>Structured pruning</em> aims to maintain the dense matrix multiplication form where some elements are zeros. They may need to follow certain pattern restrictions to work with what hardware kernel supports. Here we focus on structured pruning to achieve <em>high sparsity</em> in transformer models.</li></ul><p class="leading-8 mt-7">A routine workflow to construct a pruned network has three steps:</p><ol class="pl-8 mt-2 list-decimal"><li class="mt-3">Train a dense network until convergence;</li><li class="mt-3">Prune the network to remove unwanted structures;</li><li class="mt-3">Optionally retrain the network to recover the performance with new weights.</li></ol><p class="leading-8 mt-7">The idea of discovering a sparse structure within a dense model via network pruning while the sparse network can still maintain similar performance is motivated by <strong><a style="text-decoration: underline;" rel="noopener" title="" href="https://lilianweng.github.io/posts/2019-03-14-overfit/#the-lottery-ticket-hypothesis" target="_blank">Lottery Ticket Hypothesis</a></strong> (<strong>LTH</strong>): A randomly initialized, dense, feed-forward network contains a pool of subnetworks and among them, only a subset (a sparse network) are <em>"winning tickets"</em> which can achieve the optimal performance when trained in isolation.</p><p class="leading-8 mt-7"><em>We will continue with the Evaluation of LLMs in our next blog.</em></p><h3 id="bac9" class="font-bold font-sans break-normal text-gray-900 dark:text-gray-100 text-1xl md:text-2xl pt-12">Wrap Up!</h3><p class="leading-8 mt-3">In this blog we explored the text generation part of the Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) application, emphasizing the use of Large Language Models (LLM). It covers language modeling, pre-training challenges, quantization techniques, distributed training methods, and fine-tuning for LLMs. Parameter Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) techniques, including Adapters, LoRA, and QLoRA, are discussed. Prompting strategies, model compression methods like pruning and quantization, and various quantization techniques (GPTQ, NF4, GGML) are introduced. The blog concludes with insights into distillation and pruning for model size reduction.</p><h3 id="5052" class="font-bold font-sans break-normal text-gray-900 dark:text-gray-100 text-1xl md:text-2xl pt-12">Thank you for reading!</h3><p class="leading-8 mt-3">If this guide has enhanced your understanding of Python and Machine Learning:</p><ul class="pl-8 mt-2 list-disc"><li class="mt-3">Please show your support with a clap 👏 or several claps!</li><li class="mt-3">Your claps help me create more valuable content for our vibrant Python or ML community.</li><li class="mt-3">Feel free to share this guide with fellow Python or AI / ML enthusiasts.</li><li class="mt-3">Your feedback is invaluable — it inspires and guides my future posts.</li></ul><h3 id="ffa1" class="font-bold font-sans break-normal text-gray-900 dark:text-gray-100 text-1xl md:text-2xl pt-12">Connect with us!</h3><p class="leading-8 mt-3"><strong><a style="text-decoration: underline;" rel="noopener ugc nofollow" title="" href="https://www.linkedin.com/in/viprasingh/" target="_blank">Vipra</a></strong><strong> &amp; </strong><strong><a style="text-decoration: underline;" rel="noopener ugc nofollow" title="" href="https://www.linkedin.com/in/abhay263/" target="_blank">Abhay</a></strong></p>
        </div>

Content-Type: text/css

Content-Location: https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/highlight.js/11.9.0/styles/androidstudio.min.css

@charset "utf-8";

pre code.hljs { display: block; overflow-x: auto; padding: 1em; }

code.hljs { padding: 3px 5px; }

.hljs { color: rgb(169, 183, 198); background: rgb(40, 43, 46); }

.hljs-bullet, .hljs-literal, .hljs-number, .hljs-symbol { color: rgb(104, 151, 187); }

.hljs-deletion, .hljs-keyword, .hljs-selector-tag { color: rgb(204, 120, 50); }

.hljs-link, .hljs-template-variable, .hljs-variable { color: rgb(98, 151, 85); }

.hljs-comment, .hljs-quote { color: grey; }

.hljs-meta { color: rgb(187, 181, 41); }

.hljs-addition, .hljs-attribute, .hljs-string { color: rgb(106, 135, 89); }

.hljs-section, .hljs-title, .hljs-type { color: rgb(255, 198, 109); }

.hljs-name, .hljs-selector-class, .hljs-selector-id { color: rgb(232, 191, 106); }

.hljs-emphasis { font-style: italic; }

.hljs-strong { font-weight: 700; }
